questions.prompt: A service's p99 response time is 1.5 seconds. What does that mean?
options: The average request takes 1.5 seconds
The single slowest request took 1.5 seconds
1 in 100 requests takes at least 1.5 seconds
99% of requests take about 1.5 seconds

questions.prompt: Why is the mean a poor summary of response times?
options: It's expensive to compute over millions of requests
It ignores the fastest requests
It doesn't tell you how many users actually experienced a delay
It's always higher than the median

questions.prompt: Which percentile is the median? Answer like p95.
Loading one page makes 10 backend calls in parallel. Each backend is slow (beyond its p99) on 1% of calls. Roughly what fraction of page loads are slow?
options: About 1%
About 10%
About 0.1%
About 99%

questions.prompt: Amazon sets internal latency targets at p999 because its most valuable customers tend to make the slowest requests.
What's the difference between an SLO and an SLA?
options: An SLO measures throughput; an SLA measures latency
They're the same thing
An SLA is internal; an SLO is in the contract
An SLO is an internal goal; an SLA is a contract that promises it to customers

questions.prompt: A server's utilization climbs from 50% to 95% as traffic grows. What happens to response times?
options: They stay flat until utilization reaches 100%
They fall, because caches stay warmer under load
They rise in exact proportion to the traffic
They rise steeply, because queues form and grow faster near full capacity
